setting: A fictional office conversation about publishing a document that a generative AI tool drafted.

presentation.situation: Your colleague {{name}} wants to send out {{doc}} that an AI tool drafted. It contains {{risk}}. Help {{name}} use AI responsibly: check the content, protect private information, and be open about how it was made.
presentation.opening: I got the AI to draft {{doc}} in five minutes. It looks great, so I'm going to send it out now. Any reason not to?

brief.you_are: You are a colleague who understands the safe use of AI at work.
brief.situation: {{name}} wants to send out {{doc}} drafted by an AI tool. You can see that it contains {{risk}}, and nobody has checked it.
brief.task: Explain why it needs checking, deal with the private or unverified content, and agree how to be open about the use of AI.
brief.done_looks_like: {{name}} knows what to check, what to remove, and how to disclose AI use, and agrees to do that before sending.

participants.name: You
participants.relationship: Colleague who understands the safe use of AI

participants.name: {{name}}
participants.relationship: A colleague who is excited about AI and in a hurry

card.want: To send this today and impress the manager with how fast it was done.
card.hidden_need: Is not confident about checking figures and would welcome a simple way to do it.
card.attitude: Enthusiastic and impatient, but reasonable when given a concrete risk.
tactics: Ask 'does anyone really need to know AI wrote it?'
Accept a specific risk more readily than general warnings

pressure.gentle: Agrees quickly once a risk is explained.
pressure.balanced: Pushes back once on each point.
pressure.challenging: Argues that there is no time, and says everybody does this.

ledger.text: {{name}} used a public generative AI tool to draft {{doc}}.
Nobody has checked the draft against the source records.
{{name}} wants to send it by the end of today, and nobody has required that deadline.
{{name}} pasted the source material into the public AI tool to write the draft.

objectives.evidence: The learner explains that the content must be checked against a reliable source, and why.
alternatives: AI can sound right and still be wrong, so let's check those figures against the source

objectives.evidence: The learner identifies the private information issue, and says what to remove or how to handle it.
alternatives: Those personal details should come out, and shouldn't go into a public tool

objectives.evidence: The learner recommends appropriate disclosure and human responsibility for the final content.
alternatives: We should say AI helped draft it, and a person checked it

examples: Let's verify that against the source first.
That's personal information, so it should come out.
We should say AI helped, and that a person checked it.

beats.goal: Challenge the belief that AI output can go out unchecked.
opportunity: The AI is usually right, though. Why would I need to check it?
It looks fine to me. What could actually be wrong with it?
beats.orient: I want to send this AI draft right now without checking it. You think that's risky. Tell me why it should be checked first.
fallback: Why would I need to check it?
The AI is usually right. Isn't it?

beats.goal: Bring out the private information problem.
opportunity: I pasted everything into the tool to get this draft. That's fine, isn't it?
What about the details in it? Is there a problem with those?
beats.orient: Look at what's in the draft: {{risk}}. Tell me what's the problem with that, and what I should do about it.
fallback: Is there a problem with what's in the draft?
I pasted it all into the tool. Is that okay?

beats.goal: Settle whether to say AI was used, and who takes responsibility.
opportunity: Does anyone really need to know the AI wrote it?
If I fix it up, can't I just say I wrote it?
beats.orient: Last thing: should we tell people that AI helped, and who is responsible for what it says? Tell me what you think we should do.
fallback: Does anyone really need to know that AI wrote it?

closing_line: Okay, fair enough. I'll check it, fix it, and say how we made it.

o1.good: Explaining that AI can sound confident and still be wrong, and naming what to check against.
common_mistakes: Assuming a good-looking draft is correct
o1.micro_lesson: AI can sound certain and be wrong. Say what to check, and against which source.
o1.model: AI can sound right and still be wrong, so let's check those figures against the source records.
o1.smaller_step: Say one thing in the draft that should be checked.

o2.good: Spotting the specific private information and saying what to do with it, including what goes into public tools.
common_mistakes: Missing that pasting into the tool is itself a problem
o2.micro_lesson: Name the private detail, and say to remove it. Public AI tools are not a safe place for it.
o2.model: Those personal details should come out, and they shouldn't go into a public tool again.
o2.smaller_step: Name the private information in this draft.

o3.good: Being open that AI was used, and being clear that a person is responsible for the result.
o3.micro_lesson: Say AI helped, and make it clear that a person checked it and owns it.
o3.model: We should say AI helped draft it, and that you checked it and are responsible for it.
o3.smaller_step: Say whether people should be told AI helped.

variants.name: Zara
variants.risk: customers' personal phone numbers and two sales figures nobody has checked

variants.name: Hamza
variants.risk: named employees' private details and a claim about their results nobody has checked

variants.name: Sophie
variants.doc: a support reply to a customer
variants.risk: a refund policy that the company does not have, and a customer's home address
